summary: Describes a URN namespace for identifying content within federated content collections, which often lack a strong central authority and rely on shared naming, metadata and access conventions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Several libraries share books without one boss. This memo gives their books names that work everywhere in the group.

questions: how do content providers name resources
subtitle: A naming scheme for content in loose networks without a central authority.

tldr.problem: Federated content collections—loose networks of content providers without a single central authority—need persistent identifiers for their resources, but URLs don't work because domain ownership changes and providers come and go.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4198 establishes a URN namespace with the prefix urn:fdc: where each URI includes the provider's domain name, the date they owned that domain, and a resource ID unique to that provider and date.
tldr.outcome: Content providers in federated collections can identify resources with permanent names that survive domain ownership changes and provider transitions.

today: RFC 4198 is an Informational RFC defining a URN namespace for federated content collections that enables smaller content providers to participate in distributed systems without relying on a central naming authority.

sections.title: The Problem with Federated Content
sections.content:
Federated content collections are loose associations of content providers bound together by shared purpose but without significant central authority. Members can join or leave freely and may participate in multiple federations simultaneously. Content providers can also cease as organizations, freeing their domain names for reuse by others.

URLs don't work well in this environment because they permanently bind content to a specific domain name. When a provider's domain changes hands or is reassigned, URLs to their content become invalid. URNs provide a solution by creating permanent identifiers independent of current location.
sections.eli5: When a library moves or changes owners, the address on its books becomes wrong. URNs let you identify a book based on who owned it on what date, so the name never breaks.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content: RFC 4198 uses standard RFC 2119 terminology: MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, and OPTIONAL carry their defined meanings indicating requirement levels.
sections.eli5: The memo uses special words like MUST and SHOULD to be clear about what is required versus optional.

sections.title: URN Structure
sections.content:
Federated content URNs have the namespace ID fdc and follow the pattern urn:fdc:{ProviderId}:{DateId}:{ResourceId}.

The ProviderId MUST be an Internet domain name owned by the organization creating the resource. The DateId is a date in ISO 8601 Basic Format (YYYYMMDD or partial like YYYYMM or YYYY) corresponding to a day when the organization owned that domain name. The ResourceId MUST be unique among all resources from the same provider with the same DateId.

For example: urn:fdc:example.com:2002:A572007, urn:fdc:example.net:200406:ivr:51089, or urn:fdc:example.org:20010527:img089322-038.
sections.eli5: The pattern is: the provider's domain name, a date they owned it, and a resource number. Because you include the date, even if another company gets the domain later, old URNs still identify the original resource.

sections.title: Uniqueness and Persistence
sections.content:
The combination of ProviderId and DateId uniquely identifies the organization allocating the URN for all time. Since the organization must own the domain name on the specified date, the domain-plus-date combination serves as a permanent organizational fingerprint that cannot be reused.

Each organization is responsible for ensuring that ResourceIds are unique among all resources it allocates with that DateId. Persistence is guaranteed because the domain-plus-date combination identifies the original organization even if the domain changes hands years later.
sections.eli5: Using domain name plus date as a fingerprint means two different organizations never get the same URN, even centuries later when domain names are reused.

sections.title: Resolution and Discovery
sections.content:
Content providers are responsible for offering a URN resolution service, if any. The RFC recommends using HTTP following RFC 2169 conventions: the ProviderId (domain name) becomes the HTTP server location, allowing a resolver to find content using the domain as a starting point.

Providers should establish their own governance mechanisms to ensure identifier consistency and may provision an identifier resolution mechanism within an HTTP server designated by the ProviderId.
sections.eli5: To find a resource, you can use the domain name from the URN to contact that organization's web server and ask for the resource.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: RFC 4198 states there are no additional security considerations beyond those normally associated with URN use and resolution in general. The namespace provides persistent naming without introducing new security risks.
sections.eli5: This naming scheme doesn't create any new security dangers. It's as safe as other permanent naming systems on the internet.
